name.text: Calculating rotation in real life using wind turbines

questiontext.text:
A wind turbine has {@blades@} equally spaced blades. It completes {@rev@} complete revolution(s) every {@total_time@} minute(s).

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

A wind turbine rotates about a fixed point called its centre of rotation. One complete revolution is \(360^\circ\).

(a) Angle of rotation

The turbine completes {@rev@} revolution(s) every {@total_time@} minute(s), so it turns at a constant rate. First find the fraction of the total time that has elapsed:

\[ \frac{\text{elapsed time}}{\text{total time}} = \frac{{@elapsed@}}{{@total_time@}}. \]

In that time it completes this same fraction of its {@rev@} revolution(s). Each revolution is \(360^\circ\), so the angle turned is

\[ \frac{{@elapsed@}}{{@total_time@}} \times {@rev@} \times 360^\circ = {@angle@}^\circ. \]

\[ \boxed{ {@angle@}^\circ } \]

Note: this can exceed \(360^\circ\) — that simply means more than one full turn.

(b) Angle between adjacent blades

The {@blades@} blades are equally spaced around a full turn, so share \(360^\circ\) equally between them:

\[ \frac{360^\circ}{{@blades@}} = {@blade_angle@}^\circ. \]

\[ \boxed{ {@blade_angle@}^\circ } \]

(c) Order of rotational symmetry

The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times a shape fits onto itself during one complete turn. Rotating by {@blade_angle@}\(^\circ\) carries each blade onto the position of the next, so the turbine looks identical. Repeating this brings it back to the start after {@blades@} such rotations:

\[ \boxed{ {@order@} } \]

In general, a figure with \(n\) equally spaced identical arms has order \(n\), and the smallest turn that preserves it is \(360^\circ/n\).

(d) Does rotation change size or shape?

Rotation is a rigid transformation (an isometry): every point stays the same distance from the centre of rotation, so all lengths and angles are preserved. Only the orientation changes. The turbine before and after is therefore congruent to itself.

So the answer is \(\boxed{\text{No}}\) — neither the size nor the shape changes.

Compare: an enlargement changes size (giving a similar, not congruent, figure), while a stretch changes shape. Rotation, reflection and translation are the transformations that preserve both.

(e) Centre of rotation

The centre of rotation is the one point that does not move when the turbine turns — every other point traces a circle around it. In the diagram this is the hub where all the blades meet, at the origin:

\[ \boxed{ \text{ {@centre@} } } \]
